stem: Which choice names the two things the passage sets against each other?
stimulus: Graphene is often described as the simplest of materials: a single flat sheet of carbon atoms. Making it is anything but simple. Large sheets free of defects require extreme heat, spotless surfaces, and a delicate transfer step in which the sheet can easily tear.
choices: how hard graphene is to make and how easily its large sheets tear
how complex graphene's structure is and how easy it is to make
how simple graphene's structure is and how hard it is to make
how thin graphene's sheets are and how much heat they can withstand
explanation: The passage opens with what seems simple, graphene's structure as a single sheet of atoms. Then it turns with 'anything but simple' to what is demanding: producing the material. Choice C names both sides of that pair. This is the first step of every 'name the tension' question. Before you look at the choices, put the two sides into your own words: here, 'simple to describe' and 'hard to make'.

A.why: Both things in this choice come from the same side of the contrast, the side about how hard graphene is to make. Tearing is one of the reasons it is hard to make. You picked two details that sit together when you needed two sides that pull against each other. This is the main trap in tension questions: the choice pairs the wrong two things.

B.why: This choice swaps the two sides. The passage calls graphene's structure simple and its production hard, not the other way around. You noticed that there was a contrast but did not check which side went with which word.

D.why: The passage says that making graphene requires extreme heat. It never says the finished sheets can withstand heat. You added a property the text does not give, and you also missed the simple-versus-demanding contrast that the passage is built on.

stem: Which choice states the unintended effect of the screening policy?
stimulus: To protect young patients from infection, a hospital began screening every visitor to its children's ward for fever. Visitors who passed the check were let in without further precautions. Yet many infections spread for a day or more before any fever appears, so visitors who were already infected but not yet feverish could now walk in unmasked.
choices: Visitors who had fevers were kept out of the children's ward.
Some infected visitors reached young patients without wearing masks.
Visitors spent much longer waiting to enter the children's ward.
Every infected visitor was turned away by the new fever check.
explanation: The policy's goal was to protect young patients from infection. Its gap is that the fever check misses people who are infected but do not have a fever yet, and those people now enter without masks. So the unintended effect works against the goal: some infected visitors reach the patients the policy was meant to protect. Choice B states this. An unintended effect is usually the opposite of the policy's goal. Look for harm to the group the policy was meant to protect.

A.why: Keeping out visitors with fevers is what the policy was designed to do, so it is the intended effect. You gave the policy's goal when the question asked for the side effect nobody planned.

C.why: The passage never mentions waiting times. You picked a harm to a group the policy was not designed to protect (visitors) instead of the harm to the group it was designed to protect (young patients). This is the main trap in unintended-effect questions.

D.why: The passage says that infected visitors without a fever got past the check. 'Every infected visitor was turned away' is the opposite of that. The word 'every' should have caught your attention. Circle words like all, every and never, and check them against the text.

stem: Which choice names the disparity the passage describes?
stimulus: Recordings of everyday speech are now easy to gather: a single phone can capture hours of conversation in an afternoon. Turning those recordings into usable data is another matter. An hour of casual talk can take a trained linguist forty hours to transcribe accurately, so most recordings sit unanalyzed.
choices: Transcribing speech is quick, but recording it takes a great deal of effort.
Transcribing an hour of casual talk takes a trained linguist forty hours.
Phones capture speech accurately, but linguists capture it more accurately.
Recording speech is quick, but transcribing it takes a great deal of effort.
explanation: One side of the passage is easy: recording speech takes only a phone and an afternoon. The other side is hard: transcribing one hour of talk takes forty hours of expert work. A disparity is a gap between two things, so the answer has to name both of them in the right order. Choice D does. On the real test, this question usually appears as a blank after 'there is a disparity between...'.

A.why: This choice reverses the sides. The passage calls recording easy and transcribing slow. You found the right two activities but attached each one to the wrong side. Check both halves of a choice against the passage, not just one.

B.why: This sentence is true, but it states only the hard side. A disparity needs two things. You stopped at the striking number (forty hours) and did not include the easy side it is being compared with.

C.why: This choice pairs the wrong two things. The passage compares recording with transcribing, not phones with linguists, and it never ranks how accurately either one captures speech. You built a contrast from nouns in the passage instead of from the contrast the passage actually makes.

stem: Which choice names the risk the passage describes?
stimulus: Many stargazers assume that the brightest stars in the night sky are the most powerful. However, how bright a star looks depends on its distance as well as on the light it actually gives off. A modest star close to Earth can outshine a giant far away. Consequently, observers who judge a star's power by its brightness alone risk ______.
choices: confusing how near a star is with how powerful it is
confusing how old a star is with how powerful it is
assuming that every giant star is too distant to see
concluding that a brighter star must be a nearer one
explanation: The passage names two things that both make a star look bright: being close and being powerful. If you use brightness alone, you cannot tell which one you are seeing, so a nearby modest star can pass for a powerful one. Choice A names that exact pair. When the blank follows 'those who... risk', first identify the two things the passage says can be mixed up, then find the choice that names both of them.

B.why: The passage never mentions a star's age. You took the right structure ('confusing X with power') but filled in the wrong partner. Naming the wrong half of the pair is the main trap in this subtype.

C.why: The passage says one distant giant can look dimmer than a nearby star. It does not say every giant is too far away to see. You turned one example into a rule about all giant stars. Circle words like 'every'.

D.why: The passage describes a different mistake. Its observers treat brightness as a sign of power, not as a sign of distance. This choice describes an error the passage does not mention, and 'must' claims more certainty than the passage gives. You noticed that distance mattered but attached it to the wrong mistake.
